source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ. Ἀκουσίλαος γὰρ Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον γενέσθαι λέγει· ὅθεν καὶ ὁ τῆς Φορωνίδος ποιητὴς εἶναι αὐτὸν ἔφη πατέρα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων.
pass_a_gloss: And concerning the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews, we will speak a little later, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. For Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken in the first of his Exegetical works; however, the memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth of his Egyptian histories, although he is disposed in a rather hostile manner towards the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by race, and having even composed a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and presents Ptolemaeus of Mendes as a witness. And the words of the latter are as follows: Amosis, having become Inachus the Argive, dug up Auaria, as Ptolemaeus of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. Now this Ptolemaeus was a priest, and in three whole books he set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings, and he says that under Amosis, king of Egypt, Moses led the Jews out of Egypt, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. But the most ancient of the Greek things are the Argolic, which I call the things from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. And of these, the Attic, which are from Cecrops, the two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word, are forty generations younger; and the Arcadic, which are from Pelasgus, are nine; and this one is also said to be autochthonous. And of these, the Phthiotic, which are from Deucalion, are younger by two. And into the time of the Trojan War, twenty generations or a little more are reckoned from Inachus, and, so to speak, four hundred years. And if the Assyrian things are much older than the Greek, as Ctesias says, it will be shown that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian rule, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Beluchus, the migration of Moses from Egypt, under Amosis the Egyptian and under Inachus the Argive, took place. And in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who was after Inachus, there was the flood upon Ogygus and the kingdom in Sicyon, first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin, and the Cretan in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man to be born; hence the poet of the Phoroneis said that he, Phoroneus, was the father of mortal men.

pass_b_english: We will address the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews a little later; but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and Cassian has also spoken in the first of his Exegetical works; nevertheless, the memorandum demands that we too run through the things said here. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his Egyptian histories — although he is disposed rather hostilely toward the Hebrews, being Egyptian by race and having even composed a book against the Jews — mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events under his reign, and presents Ptolemaeus of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemaeus wrote: "Amosis, having become Inachus the Argive, dug up Auaria," as he recorded in his Chronicles. This Ptolemaeus was a priest, and in three whole books he set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings; he says that under Amosis, king of Egypt, Moses led the Jews out of Egypt, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus.

The most ancient of the Greek records are the Argolic — that is, those from Inachus — as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. Of these, the Attic, which are from Cecrops the two-natured and autochthonous, are forty generations younger, as Tatian says word for word; the Arcadic, which are from Pelasgus, are nine generations younger, and he too is said to be autochthonous. The Phthiotic, which are from Deucalion, are younger by two generations. Up to the time of the Trojan War, twenty generations or a little more are reckoned from Inachus, and, so to speak, four hundred years. If the Assyrian records are older than the Greek by many years, as Ctesias says, it will be shown that in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian rule, and in the thirty-second year of the eighth dynasty of Beluchus, the migration of Moses from Egypt took place under Amosis the Egyptian and under Inachus the Argive. In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there was the flood upon Ogygus and the kingdom in Sicyon — first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin — and the Cretan in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man to be born; hence the poet of the Phoroneis called him the father of mortal men.
